chunks: "A sample and hold is a circuit that grabs the input voltage at a specific instant and holds it steady while the ADC converts it. The simplest version is a switch and a capacitor.
When the switch is closed, which we call the track or sample phase, the capacitor charges up and follows the input.
When the switch opens, the capacitor is isolated and keeps its voltage. That's the hold phase.
Usually there's a buffer amplifier after the capacitor so whatever is reading it doesn't discharge it. Why do we need it? An ADC takes time to convert, a SAR takes N clock cycles.
If the input moves during that time, the early bits get decided at one voltage and the late bits at another, and the result is garbage. The hold freezes the value.
A rough number: a 1 kilohertz, full-scale 3. 3 volts sine moves at up to about 10 volts per millisecond, so in 78 nanoseconds it moves by one LSB of a 12-bit converter.
So the sampling instant has to be defined much more precisely than that, and the hold removes the problem for the rest of the conversion.
In a microcontroller the sampling capacitor is inside the ADC, which is why you set a sampling time and why a high-impedance source needs a longer one."
